The saturation package on three MIRI datasets: original and restored images¶

This report shows what the package (satrestore/ in this repository) does to the MIRI F2550W images of three programs on disk: cloudc and brick (program 2221) and ngc6334 (program 7213). For each dataset it puts the pipeline's original images next to the package's output on one sky mosaic, and zooms in on the saturated areas. It also covers what changed in the package since the test report (report_satrestore_test_20261029): the two defects that report found are fixed, one of its explanations is corrected, two smaller faults found while making this comparison are fixed, and a new test compares each restored pixel with the same sky in the other exposures.

Summary

  • Original against restored. Of the sky pixels that saturation left empty in the original mosaics, the package fills all 63 in cloudc, all 50 in brick, and 17,785 of 40,634 (44%) in ngc6334. The restored cores reach 2.3 to 4.2 times the brightest value the pipeline kept. What stays empty is the interior of the large saturated areas in ngc6334: there the first group lies beyond the range where the response curve passed its self-test, and the emission is too extended for a PSF fit.
  • The dark ring is fixed. Pixels flagged only because a neighbour saturated came out 0.34 dex (brick) and 0.64 dex (cloudc) darker than the measured pixels further out from the same star. The pipeline does not linearise a flagged group, and near saturation linearisation adds 22,500-30,800 DN. The package's map from raw to linearised signal stopped where each dataset's unflagged pixels stop (44,000-48,000 DN in brick and cloudc) and held its last value beyond. The map now continues to saturation with a MIRI reference map measured on ngc6334, and these pixels now sit 0.27 dex (brick) and 0.18 dex (cloudc) above the pixels further out, as pixels closer to a core should.
  • A correction to the last report. It explained the dark ring with a saturation level that varies from pixel to pixel. The saturation reference these data used (CRDS jwst_miri_saturation_0034) is 56,660 DN at every pixel, so that explanation was wrong.
  • The row-parity bias of the curve is smaller. MIRI's even detector rows saturate less uniformly than its odd rows. The response curve is now built separately for even and odd rows when both have at least 20,000 calibration rows (brick and ngc6334). In ngc6334 the even/odd difference of curve values fell from 0.052 to 0.017 dex against the neighbouring rows, and from 0.017 to 0.010 dex against the other exposures; its sign flipped, so a small difference remains. The odd-row self-test error fell to about a third; the even-row error stayed about the same.
  • New test: the same sky in other exposures. For every method and row parity, the restored pixels agree with the mean of the other exposures at the same sky position to 0.025 dex or better in median (most within 0.015), with half-widths of 0.01-0.05 dex. It also shows a parity split of the level-1 correction itself (±0.012 dex in ngc6334), which the next step addresses. This test checks consistency only: a method biased the same way in every exposure passes it, as the old dark ring did (median -0.004 dex in brick).
  • Two smaller faults fixed. The flag mask that keeps bad pixels out had two wrong bits: it excluded low-QE and RC pixels and admitted OPEN and ADJ_OPEN ones. And pixels outside the flat field (the coronagraph area, the detector edges and the defect clusters: 32% of the detector) were treated as restoration targets, although no value can be calibrated there; they now stay empty, as in the pipeline. In brick and cloudc this removed almost all "not restored" and "detector defect" counts of the last report, and all 453 "PSF fills" of ngc6334 lay there.
  • Training version. The conclusion of the last report holds: in brick the trained PSF correction moves values 0.09 dex away from the response curve, so the no-training version stays the default.

Glossary

term meaning
mosaic all exposures of a dataset on one sky grid; each sky pixel takes the mean of the exposures that have a value there
dither the small telescope offsets between exposures, which put the same sky on different detector pixels
saturated pixel a pixel that collected more charge than the detector records; the pipeline gives no value when even its first group saturated
group one of the successive reads of the detector during an integration (5, 11 or 20 here)
neighbour-flagged pixel a pixel flagged as saturated in its first group only because a neighbour saturated; its first group is a valid measurement
linearised signal the raw signal corrected for the detector's growing non-linearity near saturation; the pipeline skips this for flagged groups
raw-to-linearised map the median linearised first group as a function of the raw one, measured on unflagged pixels; the package uses it for neighbour-flagged pixels
reference map the same map measured once on ngc6334, whose unflagged pixels reach saturation; it extends each dataset's own map
level-1 pixel a pixel with only its first group below saturation; its value is corrected for the first-group bias
response curve how a pixel's raw signal grows past saturation, measured on pixels of known brightness; read backwards, it gives the brightness of a pixel saturated in its first group
q the charge in a group divided by the charge at saturation; the curve is tested up to q = 1.58 (brick, cloudc) or 2.82 (ngc6334)
row parity whether a detector row is even or odd
PSF fit the shape of a star (STPSF) fitted to the unsaturated pixels around a saturated core
detector defect a pixel flagged as saturated at the same detector position in almost every exposure
flat field the pipeline's pixel-to-pixel sensitivity map; pixels it does not cover get no calibrated value
self-test values hidden, restored and compared with the truth, on the dataset itself
half-width half the 16-84% range of a set of errors
dex a factor of 10 in log; 0.1 dex is 26%

import json, warnings
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm, ListedColormap
from matplotlib.patches import Patch, Rectangle
from astropy.io import fits
from scipy import ndimage
warnings.simplefilter('ignore', RuntimeWarning)

BLUE, ORANGE, AQUA, YELLOW, RED, PURPLE = '#2a78d6', '#eb6834', '#1baf7a', '#eda100', '#a3261f', '#7b5cc4'
INK, MUTED, GREY, LIGHT = '#0b0b0b', '#52514e', '#b5b4ae', '#e6e5e0'
EMPTY = '#1fd1e0'
plt.rcParams.update({'axes.spines.top': False, 'axes.spines.right': False, 'axes.grid': True, 'grid.color': LIGHT,
                     'grid.linewidth': 0.6, 'axes.edgecolor': GREY, 'axes.labelcolor': INK, 'xtick.color': MUTED,
                     'ytick.color': MUTED, 'lines.linewidth': 2, 'font.size': 11, 'axes.titlesize': 12,
                     'axes.titleweight': 'bold', 'legend.frameon': False, 'figure.dpi': 110})
O = '/orange/adamginsburg/w51/TaehwaYoo/w51_sat_recover/satrestore_tests'
C = f'{O}/compare'
T = ['cloudc', 'brick', 'ngc6334']
TC = {'cloudc': BLUE, 'brick': ORANGE, 'ngc6334': PURPLE}
S = {(t, m): json.load(open(f'{O}/{t}_{m}/summary.json')) for t in T for m in ['notrain', 'train']}
S1 = {t: json.load(open(f'{O}/v1/{t}_notrain/summary.json')) for t in T}
FIX = pd.concat([pd.read_csv(f'{C}/{t}_fixcheck.csv') for t in T])
DIT = pd.concat([pd.read_csv(f'{C}/{t}_dither.csv').assign(target=t) for t in T])
MOS = {(t, v): fits.getdata(f'{C}/{t}_{v}.fits') for t in T for v in ['original', 'notrain', 'train', 'notrain_v1']}
METH = {t: fits.getdata(f'{C}/{t}_method.fits') for t in T}
MC = {-1: 'white', 0: LIGHT, 1: GREY, 2: AQUA, 3: BLUE, 4: EMPTY, 5: ORANGE, 6: YELLOW, 7: RED}
LAB = {1: 'level-1 corrected', 2: 'first group linearised', 3: 'response curve', 4: 'not restored', 5: 'PSF fit', 7: 'detector defect'}
hw = lambda v: (np.percentile(v, 84) - np.percentile(v, 16)) / 2

def holes(t, v='notrain'):
    # sky pixels the pipeline left empty because they saturated (an exposure there needed a restoration method 2-6), and
    # those of them the package filled; detector defects (method 7) are counted apart
    o, n, m = MOS[t, 'original'], MOS[t, v], METH[t]
    sat = (m >= 2) & (m <= 6) & np.isnan(o)
    return sat, sat & np.isfinite(n)

def regions(t, k=2):
    # the k saturated areas with the most filled sky pixels, as (cy, cx, half-size covering the whole area)
    sat, filled = holes(t)
    lab, n = ndimage.label(ndimage.binary_dilation(sat, iterations=3))
    if not n:
        return []
    size = ndimage.sum(filled, lab, range(1, n + 1))
    out = []
    for i in np.argsort(size)[::-1][:k]:
        if size[i] == 0:
            break
        ys, xs = np.nonzero((lab == i + 1) & sat)
        h = int(np.clip(0.65 * max(np.ptp(ys), np.ptp(xs)) + 8, 18, 140))
        out.append((int(0.5 * (ys.min() + ys.max())), int(0.5 * (xs.min() + xs.max())), h))
    return out

NOVAL = {'saturated, no value': EMPTY, 'detector defect, no value': RED, 'not measured (edges, non-science area)': '#cfcdc6'}

def show(ax, img, norm, title, m):
    # m: the method mosaic on the same cut, to tell why a pixel has no value
    ax.imshow(img, origin='lower', cmap='magma', norm=norm, interpolation='nearest')
    why = np.where((m >= 2) & (m <= 6), 0, np.where(m == 7, 1, np.where(m >= 0, 2, -1)))
    for k, c in enumerate(NOVAL.values()):
        ax.imshow(np.where(np.isnan(img) & (why == k), 1., np.nan), origin='lower', cmap=ListedColormap([c]), interpolation='nearest')
    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)

1. Original and restored, dataset by dataset¶

Each dataset's exposures are put on one sky grid (nearest pixel): once with the pipeline's _cal images and once with the package's output (no-training version). Colours mark why a pixel has no value: cyan where it saturated, red where a detector defect covered it in every exposure, grey where the pipeline never measured it (mosaic edges, the coronagraph area of the detector, pixels outside the flat field). Boxes A and B mark the saturated areas shown in the zoom below each mosaic: original, package, the method that filled each pixel, and a cut through the brightest row (dotted).

In every cut, the package reads up to about 0.1 dex above the original in the pixels right next to a core where the original has a value. Those are level-1 pixels (grey in the method maps): the pipeline's value comes from their single unsaturated group and runs low, and the level-1 correction removes that bias.

    ax[r, 3].set_yscale('log'); ax[r, 3].set_xlabel('pixels from the peak (dotted row)'); ax[r, 3].set_ylabel('MJy/sr')
    ax[r, 3].set_title(f'{"ABC"[r]}: cut through the peak'); ax[r, 3].legend(loc='upper right')
fig.legend(handles=[Patch(fc=MC[k], ec=GREY, label=LAB[k]) for k in LAB] + [Patch(fc=LIGHT, ec=GREY, label='pipeline')],
           loc='lower center', ncol=7, fontsize=10.5)
plt.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.05, 1, 1)); plt.show()

Reading. One star saturates in cloudc (A), a hole of 63 sky pixels in the original. The package fills its core in rings: the response curve at the centre, the neighbour-flagged pixels (first group, linearised) around it, level-1 corrected pixels outside. The cut shows the restored profile continuing the measured wings and peaking at 47,000 MJy/sr, 2.3 times the brightest value the pipeline kept anywhere in the mosaic (20,100).

Reading. Bright extended emission saturates over large areas here; the largest (A) covers 33,000 sky pixels in the original, the next (B) 4,500. The package restores a band along the edge of each, mostly with the response curve, and the interior stays empty: there the first group lies beyond q = 2.82, the end of the curve's tested range, and the emission is too extended for a PSF fit. The cuts show the restored values continuing the measured rise into the core, up to 145,000 MJy/sr at most (4.2 times the pipeline's brightest value, 34,300). The restored band shows a fine pattern along detector rows: the row-parity effect that remains after the fix (section 2).

How much is filled¶

Counted on the sky mosaics. A sky pixel counts as saturated when it has no value in any exposure of the original and the package found it saturated in at least one exposure. "Mostly by" names the method used in most of the exposures covering the pixel; "in a few exposures only" are pixels the package restored in some exposures and left empty in most. Pixels with no value for other reasons are listed apart; neither the pipeline nor the package can give them a value.

ngc6334 has 2,255 fewer filled sky pixels than the run of the test report (20,040): more of its deep pixels now fall beyond the end of the curve's tested range (42,332 pixel-integrations against 34,778), where the package leaves them empty.

2. The two fixes¶

The dark ring around saturated cores¶

What was wrong. When a pixel saturates in its first group, the pipeline also flags its neighbours, so their first group is flagged although it is valid. The pipeline does not linearise a flagged group. The package linearised these pixels itself, with a raw-to-linearised map measured on the dataset's unflagged pixels, and then applied the level-1 correction. The flagged neighbours sit at raw 50,000-56,000 DN, where linearisation adds 22,500-30,800 DN. In brick and cloudc the unflagged pixels reach only 44,000-48,000 DN, and the map held its last value beyond that, so these pixels came out 0.34 and 0.64 dex too dark. In ngc6334 the bright extended emission samples the map up to saturation, and the same pixels were right (+0.03 dex).

The fix. The raw-to-linearised relation of the first group is a property of the detector: where the datasets overlap, brick and cloudc agree with ngc6334 to 0.0015 dex or better in the charge a first-group value carries. So the package now ships a reference map for MIRI FASTR1 full frame, measured on all 50 ngc6334 exposures up to 56,750 DN, and uses it beyond each dataset's own range. The map's self-test (half the pixels build it, the other half test it) gives half-widths of 0.0001-0.0004 dex at raw 40,000 DN and above. Where neither map has a value, the response curve restores the pixel from its own saturated groups; failing that, it stays empty.

The figure shows the brick star with the most such pixels: before, a dark ring between the core and the measured wings; after, a smooth profile. The table compares each of these pixels with the median of the measured pixels within 2 px, which lie further out on the star, so a correct value lies above them.

Row parity¶

What was wrong. In ngc6334 the curve values of even and odd detector rows differed: against the mean of the rows above and below, even rows were +0.025 dex and odd rows -0.027 dex. The cause is in how the two kinds of rows saturate. Around one shared curve, an odd-row pixel's offset has a half-width of 99 DN and repeats between exposures (correlation 0.82 between two halves of the exposures). An even-row pixel's offset has a half-width of 385 DN, with a long low tail, and does not repeat (correlation 0.16). The shared curve and its offset map averaged the two populations, which left the typical even-row pixel high and the odd-row pixel low. The calibration pixels show the same split, so the self-test can see it once it is run per row parity.

The fix. One response curve, offset map and self-test per row parity, where each parity has at least 20,000 calibration rows (brick: 211,000 and 287,000; ngc6334: 749,000 and 941,000). cloudc has 7,900 and 7,700, and keeps one shared curve. Left: the curve's self-test error by charge. Odd rows now restore to 0.009-0.023 dex in ngc6334 (one shared curve: 0.026-0.090); even rows stay at 0.027-0.078 dex, the scatter that does not repeat between exposures. Each pixel's error estimate now uses its own parity's self-test. Right: the ngc6334 curve values by row parity, before and after, against two references.

The even/odd difference shrank to about a third and changed sign. Of the curve's targets, 31% of the even-row ones and 39% of the odd-row ones are restored; the rest lie beyond the tested range.

3. The same sky in other exposures¶

The dithers put the same sky on different detector pixels, and often on rows of the other parity. For every pixel of every exposure, the test compares its value with the mean of the other exposures at the same sky position (nearest pixel). Pipeline pixels give the scale of the test itself: their medians are 0.000 dex.

Reading. Every method agrees with the other exposures to 0.025 dex or better in median, with half-widths of 0.01-0.05 dex; the PSF fit in brick is the tightest (0.011, 39 pixels). Split by row parity (tables in the appendix), the level-1 corrected pixels of ngc6334 show -0.012 dex on even rows and +0.012 dex on odd rows, and the neighbour-flagged pixels, which use the same correction, -0.019 and +0.016 dex. The first-group constants of the level-1 correction are fitted on both parities together, so they inherit the same even/odd difference the curve had. Fitting them per row parity is the next step (section 5).

This test shows consistency between exposures. A method biased the same way in every exposure passes it: the old dark ring did (-0.004 dex in brick), because every exposure's ring was dark. The self-tests and the ring check of section 2 cover bias.

4. Training against no training¶

The training version differs only where the PSF fit fills a pixel, and the PSF fit now fills only 39 pixel-integrations in brick: in cloudc no saturated core passes the point-source check, and in ngc6334 the remaining holes are extended emission. Where the PSF fit and the response curve both give a value in brick, the direct fit agrees with the curve (+0.002 dex), and the trained correction moves it to -0.091 dex, as in the last report. In ngc6334 the PSF fit runs on extended emission, and its agreement with the curve is poor either way (half-width 0.12-0.19 dex). The no-training version stays the default.

5. What is left, and next steps¶

  1. Level-1 constants per row parity. The dither test shows the level-1 correction split by ±0.012 dex between even and odd rows in ngc6334 (±0.007 in cloudc). The same per-parity treatment as for the curve applies, with the same 20,000-pixel rule; the calibration pixels of the curve take their brightness from this correction, so the curve gains too.
  2. The empty interiors in ngc6334 (22,849 sky pixels). There the first group lies beyond the q range the curve passed its self-test on, and these datasets cannot test higher q. Options: a cross-filter fill from the program's other filters, with the spread threshold from the generalization report; or a longer tested range from datasets with more groups.
  3. Even detector rows. Their scatter near saturation does not repeat between exposures, so no per-pixel calibration removes it. The error each restored pixel carries now reflects it, and combining dithered exposures averages it down.
  4. The reference map covers MIRI FASTR1 full frame. Other readouts and subarrays need their own map, from a bright dataset of that readout or from the CRDS linearity reference.
  5. More data. Other MIRI filters of these programs, the sgrb2 data (needs the stage-1 pipeline first), and a NIRCam program for the first-read method.
  6. Packaging. Install the package (pip install -e satrestore) and run it from the command line on a new dataset, outside this repository.

Appendix. Numbers, files, and what was not checked¶

Package changes since the test report (commits in this repository): curve per row parity (446fea2, 96e99da); neighbour-flagged pixels through the raw-to-linearised map within its range, the curve otherwise (93ca5b1); the MIRI reference map satrestore/satrestore/data/miri_group0_map_fastr1.csv (dce888f); level-1 self-test without NaN (f27f834, 7e5ca0a); the flag mask and the flat-field area (5cdf612).

Files. Runs in /orange/adamginsburg/w51/TaehwaYoo/w51_sat_recover/satrestore_tests/<target>_<notrain|train>/; the runs of the test report in v1/. Mosaics, method maps, the dither test and the ring check in compare/ (<target>_original.fits, _notrain.fits, _train.fits, _notrain_v1.fits, _method.fits, _dither.csv, _fixcheck.csv), made by compare.py and fixcheck.py. Diagnostics: diag_fgl.py (dark ring), diag_parity2.py to diag_parity6.py and diag_l1parity.py (row parity), diag_mapshare.py (map across datasets), build_group0_ref.py (reference map). Report builder: make_report_compare.py with report_compare_text.py.

Not checked. The mosaics use the nearest pixel, so a sky position can shift by up to half a pixel between exposures; this widens the dither test near steep cores but does not bias it. The reference map is measured on one program; brick and cloudc confirm it only up to 47,750 DN. The even-row scatter was examined in ngc6334 and brick only.

The tables below give the curve self-tests by row parity, the raw-to-linearised map's self-test, and the dither test by method and parity (before = the run of the test report, after = this one).
